# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to face its star eternally while the other remains in perpetual darkness. This phenomenon, common among close-orbiting exoplanets, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in continuous stellar radiation, can reach scorching temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out entirely. On a tidally locked planet without sufficient atmosphere, the temperature difference between the two hemispheres could exceed several hundred degrees.

Atmospheric circulation becomes the planet's lifeline. On Earth, sunlight strikes everywhere over a day-night cycle, but on a tidally locked world, air on the dayside heats and rises, flows toward the nightside, cools and sinks, then returns along the surface—a permanent convection cell. Climate models suggest that a dense atmosphere or deep ocean can redistribute heat effectively enough to keep the terminator—the twilight zone between hemispheres—potentially habitable.
